messages.subject: Puzzlement over vectorization in BUGS epil example
parts:
Greetings, folks:  Back for more help.  I am having difficulty visualizing how the vectorized commands are working in the epil example (Book 1 of the old BUGS examples).  This is a mixed Poisson model.  (Ancient history, I know.  But the great masters tried to understand historical models before doing something "original.")

In this example, there are N (59) subjects, each seen T (4) times.  The dependent variable  y is declared in a 59 x 4 matrix.  Other covariates (constant within subject) are given in length 59 vectors.  There is an indicator variable for the fourth visit (all other visits are treated the same).  So visit number is given as a length four vector (0,0,0,1).  The data are eventually all centered, but that is, I think, irrelevant to my question.  b and b1 are two variance variables to be estimated for the patient and the patient * visit levels.  a0 and Alphas are all parameters to be fitted.  After various declarations and data manipulation, the final model is given as:

for(n in 1:N) {
    b[n] ~ normal(0, sigma_b);
    y[n] ~ poisson_log(a0 + alpha_Base * log_Base4_c[n]
                          + alpha_Trt * Trt_c[n]
                          + alpha_BT  * BT_c[n]   //log(Base) * trt
                          + alpha_Age * log_Age_c[n]
                          + b1[n] + alpha_V4 * V4_c + b[n]);
  }

My confusion comes in the last line.  There are 59 * 4 observations, with no missing values, and I am assuming that a (perhaps virtual) 59 * 4 matrix of predictors for each subject is being created.  I assume that a 59 * 4 length y vector is being created for each patient and each visit.  Since R and STAN go by column major order, the y vector holds the value for the first visit for each patient, then for the second visit for each patient, and so forth.  No problem with the vectors for the various columns of of patient level data.  Each column is just repeated four times, lining up correctly with the y's.  But the V4_c  variable is only length 4.  It should be repeated 59 times, but with as "rep(V4_c, each = 59), rather than as "rep(V4_c, 59) which would assign the indicators for the V4 visit incorrectly.  Since "V4_c" is referenced in the last line without any indices, how does the code know to create a column of "rep(v4_c, each = 59)" rather than rep(V4_c, 59), i.e., the length four V4c vector repeated 59 times? 

And am I visualizing correctly how the final design matrix and dependent variable vector are being created?

Thanks in advance for your help with my confusion.

Larry Hunsicker

Bob:
My apologies for being unclear in my last post.  Let me try to ask my question in a way that I hope is closer to correct.  b1 is intended to be the patient level residual and b the residual patient * visit residual, to account for extra Poisson variability.  Neither of these is an input value.  They are both declared to be draws from normal 0 mean distributions with sd's = sigma_b1 and sigma_b, respectively. 
My question is not how these values are fit by STAN, but only about how STAN knows that b1 is the patient level residual and b the patient by visit residual.  My guess is that this is because b1 is declared OUTSIDE of the do-loop, so that it sees that it has N levels, whereas b is declared INSIDE of the do-loop, so that it sees that, at each level of N, there are four (visit) levels.  I think that this is corroborated by the fact that at each draw, STAN draws N sample values for b1, but N * 4 values for b. 
At this point of my STAN learning curve, I don't need to know how STAN figures out the densities.  That comes later after I have made more progress through Gelman et al.  All I need to understand better today is how to code this sort of nested mixed model correctly.
Again, thanks for your help, your availability, and (I hope) your patience with me.
Larry

On Tuesday, June 16, 2015 at 7:28:02 PM UTC-4, Larry Hunsicker wrote:
My question is not how these values are fit by STAN, but only about how STAN knows that b1 is the patient level residual and b the patient by visit residual.  My guess is that this is because b1 is declared OUTSIDE of the do-loop, so that it sees that it has N levels, whereas b is declared INSIDE of the do-loop, so that it sees that, at each level of N, there are four (visit) levels.  I think that this is corroborated by the fact that at each draw, STAN draws N sample values for b1, but N * 4 values for b.

What Bob was saying is that Stan (unlike BUGS) does not infer the number of elements in b and b1 from whether they are outside or inside some loop but simply accepts the dimensions that the user declares in the Stan program. In the epil example,

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/stan-dev/example-models/master/bugs_examples/vol1/epil/epil.stan

we have in the parameters block

...
real  b1[N]; 
vector[T] b[N];
...

so b1 has N elements and b has T * N elements regardless of what goes on in the subsequent blocks.

Ben

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Puzzlement over vectorization in BUGS epil example
parts:
On Wednesday, June 17, 2015 at 6:56:10 PM UTC-4, Larry Hunsicker wrote:
Based on yesterday's discussion, I thought that I understood that the prior for b: "b[n] ~ normal(0, sigma_b);" could be put pretty much anywhere, since the shape of b had been set by its earlier declaration in the parameters section.

It is true that the dimensions of b are declared in the parameters section, but a for-loop in Stan

  for(n in 1:N) {
b[n] ~ normal(0, sigma_b);

...

works like a for-loop in any other language. Here it indicates that the n-th element of b --- which happens to be a vector of length T in this case --- has a prior on its elements that is iid normal with mean zero and standard deviation sigma_b.
  • If you put anything involving b[n] outside the for loop, Stan wouldn't know what n refers to.
  • b[N][K] ~ normal(0, sigma_b) does not make much sense because it puts the normal(0, sigma_b) prior only on the N,K element and does not put a proper prior on any of the other elements (which is why it took a long time to sample)

There are some ways that this could be improved upon:

  • Delete the line that says b[n] ~ normal(0, sigma_b); and add (outside the for loop) the line to_array_1d(b) ~ normal(0, sigma_b);. This concatenates all the elements of b into a one-dimensional array and asserts the prior is iid normal with mean 0 and standard deviation sigma_b.
  • Delete the line that says b[n] ~ normal(0, sigma_b); and the line that says b1 ~ normal(0, sigma_b1); Add (outside the for loop) the line to_array_1d(b) ~ normal(0, 1); and the line b1 ~ normal(0,1). Finally, change the last line of the likelihood to say + b1[n] * sigma_b1 + alpha_V4 * V4_c + b[n] * sigma_b); . This basically redefines b[n] and b1 to be standard normal shifts that are scaled by the unknowns sigma_b and sigma_b1 respectively, which often improves the efficiency of the sampling by reducing the dependence between these unknown parameters.

You can always print things to the screen if you are having trouble understanding the structure:

print("b is");
for(n in 1:N) print(b[n]);
but something like that is best called in diagnostic mode (in R with test_grad = TRUE and chains = 1) so that you only see it once rather than millions of times.


Ben

parts:
Thanks, Andrew:

The code is all based on the old BUGS examples, and all the BUGS examples seem to use those very wide priors.  I have fiddled with the normal priors and agree that normal(0, 10), or even normal(0,2) seem to give very similar posteriors to normal(0, 100) for, e.g. sd of average height of women in meters.  But I haven't got to learning about sensible non- or weakly- informative priors yet.  Maybe I should just switch over to the ARM examples to learn from.  I promise not to use inv_gamma(.001, .001) ever again. 

Larry Hunsicker
